newsitem.title: GERMANY: Trade sees pressure on German wheat prices.
newsitem.headline: Trade sees pressure on German wheat prices.

text.p: German wheat prices are likely to fall to match lower consumer offers, traders at a northern European industry meeting said on Tuesday.
"European millers and feed mixers are reducing their buying prices and trade buying from farms and cooperatives is very slow," one trader said.

"Milder weather will free up transport capacity as rivers and canals are thawing and that takes the urgency out of spot business," he said as some 380 traders gathered for the Hamburg Grain and Feeds Association's new year meeting.
"I believe there will be heavy losses in wheat this year."
Steadying factors were hopes of sales to Uzbekistan in February and March, when Poland might also re-emerge as a buyer, and the strength of sterling, which might block out British feed wheat.
German prices were well above French and British levels because of farmer hoarding and speculative trade buying from the 1996 harvest following a period of high prices.
"Farmer retention will turn out to be the wrong policy as prices look set to fall, not rise," said Christof Buchholz, the new managing director of the hosting Hamburg trade association.

Buchholz said traders were generally content with the pace of export licensing by the European Union, with levels in the 1996/97 season to date of roughly 17 million tonnes compared with 18 million in the full 1995/96 season.
EU traders hope exports will reach between 25 and 29 million tonnes by the end of the marketing year.
"But that could still leave us with 10 million tonnes of grain in intervention stores," a trader said.
"The problem is that exports to third countries will be mostly made from France, while the bulk of the volumes sold into intervention will be stored in Germany."
For example, Germany accounted for only 1,000 tonnes out of the 260,000 tonnes of free market wheat export subsidies given by EU cereals managers at last week's tender, he said.
A cut in the set-aside rate for 1997 harvesting meant another huge EU grain crop this year would add to supply.
In the fob Baltic export market, brokers put normal spot bread wheat (12 percent protein) for second half January at a little changed 286-287.50 marks this week.
They kept higher quality offers steady on the week at around 292-308, depending on protein levels.
Fob Baltic barley was quoted 2.50-3.00 marks higher at 257.50-274 marks, boosted by expectations of a large EU barley inclusion in Saudi Feb/March purchases of 1.2 million tonnes.
Fob rye offers were up 1.50-3.00 marks at 254-268 marks after domestic millers bought some bread rye.
European meals and feeds market were as much as $3 per tonne higher this morning in sympathy with rallies in Chicago soybean and products markets as well as a firm dollar.
"Feed grain is the cheapest ingredient in feed mixes while protein feeds are being ignored, apart from some spot business," one meals broker said.
Spot Hamburg soymeal (44 percent) was at 47.50 marks fob, up from 47.25 on Monday and 45.50 marks last Friday.
Rapeseed sellers were at 475 marks, up from 470 on Friday.
